source.citation: Richet, P. (1987). Heat capacity of silicate glasses. Chemical Geology 62, 111-124.

transcription.from: the published article (publisher's PDF), Tables I and A-I read on the pages rendered at 150-200 dpi
transcription.note: Table I prints its columns as a_i, 10^3 b_i, 10^-5 c_i and d_i; the values here are b_i and c_i themselves. Its footnote 1: for oxides not in the table, use the heat capacity of the crystalline phase; footnote 4: the SiO2 row is the heat capacity of pure SiO2 glass (Richet et al. 1982); footnote 5: the B2O3 row is that of pure B2O3 glass. The model of the paper is Cp = sum_i x_i Cp_i (Eq. 1), x_i the mole fraction of oxide i in the glass, each Cp_i = a_i + b_i T + c_i/T^2 + d_i/T^0.5 (Eq. 3), and H_T - H_T0 = sum_i x_i int Cp_i dT (Eq. 4); it holds below the glass transition, to about 1 % (abstract and p. 111). The H2O coefficients come from one study on one glass, and the paper says their accuracy is not warranted (p. 115). Integrating Table I over 273-1000 K reproduces the five enthalpies of Table A-I within -0.6 to +0.7 %.

oxide_heat_capacity.location: Table I, p. 114: partial molar heat capacities of the oxides in silicate glasses, the temperature interval of the data used (Delta T) and the range of mole fractions (Delta x, mol%) of each oxide in the data of Table II

relative_enthalpies.location: Table A-I, p. 121: compositions (mol%) and relative enthalpies of five aluminosilicate glasses, from fitted equations that reproduce the measurements between 900 and 1050 K within 0.05 %

notes: The relative enthalpies of Table A-I are per mole of the glass written as one mole of oxides (the mole fractions of the table summing to one), as the heat capacities of Eq. (1).
